summary: Psalm 130 begins with a cry from “the depths” and asks the Lord to hear. The speaker faces the problem of sins, rests hope on forgiveness, waits for Yahweh like watchmen waiting for morning, and then calls Israel to hope in Yahweh’s loving kindness and redemption.
whyItMatters: This psalm gives Book V a compact prayer of distress, confession, waiting, and communal hope. It shows how the Psalter can move from one voice in need to a word addressed to all Israel.

context.author: The psalm itself names no individual author. Its heading calls it “A Song of Ascents,” one of the collection labels preserved in the Psalter.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: The Psalter is an anthology formed over time; this psalm’s precise date is uncertain.
context.setting: The psalm does not name a location. It speaks from deep distress and turns toward Israel as a worshiping community.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, using direct address, repeated waiting language, and a movement from individual petition to communal exhortation.

outline.heading: A Cry From the Depths
outline.note: The speaker cries to Yahweh and asks the Lord to listen attentively to petitions.

outline.heading: Sin and Forgiveness
outline.note: The psalm asks who could stand if Yah kept a record of sins, then answers with forgiveness that leads to fear.

outline.heading: Waiting for the Lord
outline.note: The speaker waits and hopes in Yahweh’s word, longing more intensely than watchmen wait for morning.

outline.heading: Israel Called to Hope
outline.note: The individual prayer widens into a call for Israel to hope in Yahweh, because loving kindness, abundant redemption, and rescue from sins are with him.

keyVerses.text: If you, Yah, kept a record of sins, Lord, who could stand?
keyVerses.why: This question names the crisis beneath the prayer: no one can stand before God if sins are kept on record.

keyVerses.text: But there is forgiveness with you, therefore you are feared.
keyVerses.why: The psalm’s answer is not denial of sin but forgiveness with God, which produces reverent fear.

keyVerses.text: I wait for Yahweh. My soul waits. I hope in his word.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the posture at the center of the psalm: waiting, longing, and hope grounded in Yahweh’s word.

keyVerses.text: Israel, hope in Yahweh, for there is loving kindness with Yahweh. Abundant redemption is with him.
keyVerses.why: The prayer turns outward here, inviting Israel to share the speaker’s hope in Yahweh’s loving kindness and redemption.

questions.question: What are “the depths”?
questions.answer: The psalm does not define the phrase as a specific place or event. In verse 1 it names the speaker’s condition as deep distress, from which the cry goes up to Yahweh.

questions.question: Who is speaking in the opening verses?
questions.answer: The first voice is an individual “I” who has cried to Yahweh and asks the Lord to hear. By verse 7 the psalm turns from that individual voice to Israel, so the prayer becomes communal without losing its personal beginning.

questions.question: Why does the psalm ask, “who could stand?”
questions.answer: Verse 3 imagines Yah keeping a record of sins and asks who could remain standing under that scrutiny. The question expects a sobering answer: no one can rely on innocence before God in that way.

questions.question: Does “feared” mean terror?
questions.answer: Verse 4 connects fear with forgiveness, not with God keeping an unforgiving record. In this psalm, fear means reverent seriousness before the God who forgives; it is not described as panic or moral despair.

questions.question: What does it mean to wait for Yahweh?
questions.answer: Verses 5-6 describe waiting as active hope and longing. The speaker’s soul waits and hopes in Yahweh’s word, then compares that longing to watchmen waiting for morning.

questions.question: Why are watchmen mentioned?
questions.answer: The watchmen image gives the reader a concrete picture of tense, expectant waiting for morning. The psalm does not specify a military or city scene in detail; it uses the image to intensify the speaker’s longing for the Lord.

questions.question: Why does the psalm move from “I” to “Israel”?
questions.answer: The psalm begins with one speaker’s cry, but it ends by addressing the whole community. The experience of sin, forgiveness, waiting, hope, and redemption is presented as more than a private matter.

questions.question: What is hard about saying God will redeem Israel “from all their sins”?
questions.answer: The promise reaches all Israel’s sins, but the psalm does not explain the timing or manner of that redemption. Verses 7–8 ground Israel’s hope in Yahweh’s loving kindness and abundant power to redeem. The confidence rests with God rather than with Israel’s ability to erase its own record.

glossary.def: The heading shared by Psalms 120–134. It identifies this psalm’s collection without specifying its original performance setting.
The deep distress from which the speaker cries to Yahweh in verse 1.
Requests or pleas addressed to the Lord in verse 2.
People used in the psalm’s comparison for eager waiting until morning.
The quality said to be with Yahweh in verse 7, paired there with abundant redemption.
The deliverance or rescue said to be abundant with Yahweh and promised for Israel from all their sins.
